HEADLINE: Golden age
TEXT:
Dream in Paris, live in New York. That was Baz Luhrmann’s philosophy, until twists of fate brought him to the Gold Coast to create his upcoming film on Elvis. And having looked around, he likes what he sees.

“The philosophy of my company is communication, transportation, accommodation – hair ...” It’s early afternoon, the fifi rst quarter of a day that started with pilates and will end somewhere after midnight.

Dressed in what would be a tracksuit on anyone else, white curls gathered in an accordion headband, Baz Luhrmann is draped across an overstuffed sofa.

“Hair’s a joke,” he clarififi es as I eye his. “It just means wellbeing. Feeling good about yourself.”

He is running me through the logic of the room we have just sat down in, a free-standing cabana on a raised platform, doors and ceiling draped, a porcelain tiger the size of a house cat prowling the coffee table between us. “I call this Faisal’s Tent,” he says, a reference to the princely tabernacle in which T.E. Lawrence meets the leader of the Arab Rebellion in David Lean’s 1962 classic. “You can’t create if you’re not in an environment that feels creative. Fear’s the enemy of any creative venture; all of the greats I’ve worked with have it; it’s why they’re great. So we put as much energy into making an environment conducive to imagination; I like to say ‘keeping fear at bay’.”

That is an understatement. Pitched in a former car park, Faisal’s Tent is one flfl ank of the mini-Xanadu Luhrmann and his wife and collaborator, Catherine Martin, have conjured on an unremarkable stretch of the long, flfl at Gold Coast Highway in Miami, Queensland. From the outside, the building looks exactly like what it was: a long, single-storey, brickand- steel Australian Federal Police headquarters.

Open the double doors, however, and you enter Elvisville. Portraits from The King’s lushest periods line the walls. Martin-designed Presley board games, complete with token and card (“no detail too small,” says Luhrmann) are stacked against a wall. Past reception, you enter a Graceland mashup, one wall covered in mock movie posters, The King’s face replaced with that of the young American actor, Austin Butler, who beat the likes of Harry Styles to the role. They’re the work of Butler’s co-star Tom Hanks, made to encourage the ingenu. “Tom’s such a team player,” Luhrmann says approvingly.

On the right, enfilade doors give onto a raked editing theatre, modelled on Elvis’ Hilton suite during his legendary, ruinous 636-show Las Vegas residency. Since March this year, Luhrmann and a team of 40 have been hunkered down here, completing the director’s biopic of the singer, his first film since The Great Gatsby in 2013. And it says everything about nowthat a film about a quintessentially American star, a man who only ever left the US once, on military service, is being made by an Australian, with an Australian crew, on the Gold Coast.

First announced in 2014, shooting finally began in January 2020 before being shut down in March when Hanks, who plays Presley’smanager Colonel Tom Parker – “he was never a colonel, never a Tom, never a Parker,” Luhrmann quips – became Hollywood’s first COVID-19 poster boy. Even in postproduction, the director is still keeping fear at bay. “I never know. I never know,” he says when asked if he’s happy with the film, paused on screen when we firstmeet in the theatre.

“I can tell you though, and I don’t say this lightly, that I have absolutely no doubt about the quality of the performances of my two leads, who have to carry this story.”

More broadly, too, the past 18 months have been particularly interesting for a man who made his name reimagining a world of which he could only dream growing up in the tiny town of Herons Creek on the NSW North Coast. A man who has infused the classics of that world – from Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet to Dumas’ The Lady of the Camellias and Fitzgerald’s Gatsby – with the heightened romance of that longing. Onewho has sincemade thatwider world his home, living in New York while simultaneously racking up the second-longest residency at the Chateau Marmont in LA (beaten only by HelmutNewton’s widow).As Luhrmann says, “I have a philosophy: dream in Paris, dance in Brazil, have fun in London and work in LA. Australia’s always home, but live in New York.”

Of course,COVID-19 stopped that music dead. Andwhen it did, Luhrmann found himself a few hundred kilometres up the highway from where he’d started. By the time he leaves Queensland, he will have been on the Goldie for two years, “the longest I’ve been in one place since I was 18,” he says.

He’s not one for looking back, but the experience has clearly given him pause. Time to look around.

And what he’s seen is opportunity. A historic opportunity for Australia to finally fulfil its potential as a film production centre.Potential as tantalisingandmonumentaltoLuhrmann as a half-written story. “There was a time when movies were only made in New York,” he says, once-upon-a-timing it.

“Then someone said ‘look, there’s this place called California, there’s a lot of cattle farms but it’s quite sunny and really good for making movies’. So they travelled out west and made a place called Hollywood. For me, this feels a bit like that.

“I really think the Gold Coast is particularly engineered for filmmaking. I love Sydney, but it’s a bit like New York: it’s a financial centre; it’s a political centre. It can’t be wholly devoted to sports and entertainment. Like in LA, filmmaking and tourism are natural bedfellows because you’re building fantasy, escapism. A story.”

Luhrmann only ended up on the Gold Coast by accident.

He shot both Moulin Rouge! and Gatsby at Sydney’s Fox Studios, which he had played a role in founding. But Disney, which bought 21st Century Fox from Rupert Murdoch in 2019, has the studios solidly booked.WhenFoxwas no longer an option, Queensland Premier Annastacia Palaszczuk won Luhrmann over. “I absolutely loved her can-do energy,” he says. “She said, ‘Look, just go and visit’. My memory of the Goldie was meter maids.” What he found was a hipster capital still in the process of writing its story, a “paradise” to which he would return to in a heartbeat, Luhrmann says.

Right now though, paradise is full. As Luhrmann vacated Queensland’s Village Roadshow studios, Ron Howard – as fast at making movies as Luhrmann is slow – started shooting his Thai-cave-rescue flick. Because all nine sound stages were busy at Village – the southern hemisphere’s largest studio – Chris Hemsworth had to shoot his Netflix sci-fi adventure Escape from Spiderhead at the Gold Coast Convention and Exhibition Centre.

Nor is it just the Goldie. Down the road in northern NSW, Byron Baes, Netflix’s first Australian reality TV series, has been shooting in Hemsworth’s hometown, where Nine Perfect Strangers, executive-produced for Hulu by Big Little Lies’ Nicole Kidman and Bruna Papandrea, recently wrapped. Further south, George Miller completed filming Three Thousand Years of Longing in December, and will next year start shooting his Fury Road prequel Furiosa, billed the biggest film ever made in Australia. Marvel’s Thor: Love And Thunder, starring Chris Hemsworth, Matt Damon and Natalie Portman, has also been filming in Sydney since January, as has Papandrea’s eight-part series Pieces of Her starring Toni Collette.

In fact, Disney is reportedly planning to relocate Marvel’s HQ from Atlanta to Sydney. That has forced Miller, too, to improvise in a converted warehouse elsewhere in the city.

Meanwhile, the Liam Neeson feature Blacklight began shooting in Victoria late last year and the BBC One/Stan coproduction, The Tourist, starring Jamie Dornan, has been filming in South Australia.

Therecentmomentumhasn’tcomeentirely outof theblue.

Elder statesmen like Luhrmann and Miller have brought production home through the decades, thanks to the federal government’s generous producer offset for Australian-led films. More recently, heavyweights like Hemsworth and Kidman have followed their lead. In part, it’s karma for the talent this country has bred, trained and exported over the years, not least to Hollywood.

What secured those projects pre-pandemic, however, was the 13.5 per cent location incentive the federal government introduced in 2018 after significant lobbying to make Australia competitive in the global location game.

As the world shut down, the government slung another $400 million into the pot in July 2020 to lure the footloose production that’s since flooded in.

As Luhrmann sees it, though, “the tectonic plates were already on the move” even before those lures. “And that’s a rhythm of history,” he adds. “It doesn’t happen every 10 years, it might happen every 100 years.”

Competition between the proliferating streaming services alone has spawned a content arms war. Disney announced in December that it planned to spend about $US15 billion ($20 billion) a year across streaming services, including Hulu and Disney+, and ramp up original content to 100 titles a year, including its Marvel and Star Wars brands. In May, Amazon Prime announced itwould plough $150million into content produced in Australia alone. The result has “been a global shortage of studio infrastructure for years, driven by the sheer increase in content being made,” says KateMarks, CEO of Ausfilm. “It’s very difficult to get studio spaces at the moment in the UK, for example, which is booked out well in advance, and every week there seems to be new infrastructure coming online around the world.”

Which brings us back to Faisal’s Tent. “This is a postproduction facility, but I had to build it,” Luhrmann says of theMiami workaround. “I also have a space in Brisbane and a mixing stage in Sydney upgraded by a very entrepreneurial fellow, so I can mix a big film here.” To capitalise on the opportunity that now presents itself, he says, what Australia needs is not just clear, consistent, dependable state and federal incentives to feed the production pipeline, but the facilities tomakefilmmakinghereanend-to-endproposition, from development, through production to post-production.

“Australia is great for shooting but why let the talent and the energy and the money dribble out the door, because we can’t start or finish [projects]?” Luhrmann says, adding: “But to be honest, we’ve always been like this. We’re the same with our primary industries. We could have not only grown the sheep, sheared the sheep, but also [manufactured and designed]. Or mining, we’re happy to rip stuff out of the ground and send it off, as opposed to beginning to end.”

Which is the real jeopardy in the current equation as he sees it. Not that production will stop flowing Down Under.

Everyone knows COVID-19 was an anomaly, though Marks says Ausfilm, which promotes Australia internationally as a destination, is “still seeing solid inquiries in for the back end of this year and into 2022. If incentives stay in place, there will be a consistent level of production coming down.”

Screen Australia CEO Graeme Mason agrees: “We have an enormous opportunity, but it’s up to us to build on the fact that everyone has discovered us,” he says. “We’re Englishspeaking, we’re a safe location, and we’re a location most people want to go to once. Once they come down here they find our crews and facilities are amazing. And how integrated we already are into Hollywood.”

To Luhrmann, the real risk is that we won’t make the most of our current advantage. Australia’s cultural development has always been fitful, he says, characterised by breakthrough moments of vision, purple patches of support for culture that tend to dissipate into longueurs of inaction.

“There is a particular Aussie creativity that I refer to as ‘flashes of lightning’,” he says. “I mean, look at the Sydney skyline, pretty generic and then boom, flash of lightning, the Opera House.Where did that come from?” Luhrmann and Martin were themselves the product of such a moment. Their breakthrough 1990 Opera Australia production of La Bohème came in the same year the Hawke government, having boosted arts funding 40 per cent in three years, took direct funding control and gave it an extra $1 million. The couple were swept into a moment of cultural priority and confidence, like Barrie Kosky, who would go on to become a star opera director. “We were doing radical operas here, us and Barrie,” Luhrmann says. “Because the arts were really well-funded and supported, and we were really into it.”

That experimentation in turn helped fuel international revolutions in not just opera but film. Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet applied the same luridly contemporising approach to the Bard. And you can trace the shadow of La Bohème’s “L’amour” sign, inspired by the Coke sign in Sydney’s Kings Cross, throughout Luhrmann’s career, from Moulin Rouge! to his 2004 ad for Chanel No.5. Not to mention the influence of opera’s fundamental grounding in music as the engine of drama.

The love sign would be echoed too in the 1993 campaign launch that Luhrmann – freshly famous from 1992’s Strictly Ballroom – stage-managed for Paul Keating, the word AUSTRALIA emblazoned across a cobalt curtain.

In the wake of Keating’s unlikely “true believers” victory, Luhrmann lobbied the PM for a city film studio in Sydney.

“I said: Look, very few cities in the world have a studio right in the middle of the city,” he recalls. “You don’t know what that means to filmmaking.” Fox would be announced a year later as part ofAustralia’s first major cultural policy, the fouryear, $250 million Creative Nation strategy, which Keating hoped would draw a line under “our post-colonial era” and say “goodbye to it”.

“I always felt that Australia would have its very particular moment,”Luhrmannsays. “Which iswhy Iwas so passionate about becoming a republic. People think that’s just a symbol but it’s not. Surely we’re mature enough to elect our head of state?” It’s that sort of maturity that is on offer – but also required – now, he says. “It has to stop being flashes of lightning. There needs to be consistent, concerted policy and incentives but also consistent infrastructure.”

It’s the sort of strategic, long-term thought and investment for which George Miller has been calling for a decade now, not just to maximise the economic impact of films made here, but also to give the talent Australia mints and exports a long-term, stable home base from which to work. And the day after the Financial Review speaks to Luhrmann, another Australian star, Russell Crowe, does something about it, announcing he’s backing a $438 million fully integrated feature-film production and post-production complex down the road from the Goldie in Coffs Harbour, another town built, LA-like, around a highway.

“Whatever your thoughts on a higher power, they’re a great stage manager, a great writer,” Luhrmann says. We’re discussing his personal revolution of the past 18 months. “I mean, you couldn’t write this. Just when I think I’ve seen or experienced it all, I end up making a film about Elvis by myself on the Gold Coast – and being wowed by it.

It’s energised, enlivenedme to findmyself atmy age back in a place not unlikewhere Igrewup,”he says. “I really surf change ... the energy never scares me. I love to be lifted up by it.”

In many ways the Gold Coast has been eerily familiar.

Not only is it a few hours’ drive from Herons Creek, but the couple have found the maximalist fabrics, wallpapers and rugs Martin began designing more than a decade ago for retail are everywhere, as if she’d already art-directed it.

But then 2021 has been a year of milestones: a quarter of a century since Romeo + Juliet,which divided critics but is now regarded as a milestone adaptation; 20 years since Moulin Rouge! single-handedly revived the fortunes of the movie musical, an artform Luhrmann had been warned was dead.

And by the time Elvis makes it to cinemas in 2022, Strictly Ballroom, his first film, made at just 29, will turn 30. Does he feel vindicated? “I’m much more focused on what’s in front of me,” he says. “Letme tell you, as soon as you get towhere I am, you forget about it. I feelmuseummoments occasionally, but honestly, inmy soul, I feel like I’mjust getting going and haven’t donemuch yet.”

Luhrmann did though recently revisit the problem child of his oeuvre, 2008’s Australia, working with Hulu on an asyet unannounced long-play version titled Faraway Downs, which he says will tease out some of the larger themes the film couldn’t. Whatever Australia’s merits – and he’s frank it “really didn’t land in the US” where it matters – he always intended the film tomake a statement not just about, but to, this country. “I’mnot saying thatAustralia or FarawayDowns are in themselves the singular gesture of self-reflection or a maturing attitude,” he says. “But I didwant to take [on] some of the more difficult issues and realities of our history, and in a broad way that allowed as many people into it as possible, rather than a film that would be seen by a very limited audience.”

In the same way he took on Elvis, he says, not so much for the singer as the times he sang. “When I look at musical biography, it’s not really about the life,”he says. “I’mnot about lionising Elvis. I just saw him as the best canvas on which to explore America in the modern age, the ’50s, ’60s and ’70s.” The engine of that drama, he says, is the relationship between an artist who spanned genres, eras and races, and the P.T. Barnum character of Colonel TomParker, the former circus carny who made and then ruined him.

“I saw this story of the Colonel and Elvis as a really great prism through which to explore the latter part of the 20th century,” Luhrmann says. “Elvis represents what happens when a kid lives in one of four designated white houses in a black community. Something new comes about, a fusion between country and African-American music, gospel and country-and-western music.TheColonel represents that other quality in America, ‘the big sell’. The tension between the two is great when they’re in balance. But when they’re thrown out of balance, and it just becomes about exploiting and selling and ceases to be creative, then the world’s out of whack ... and theworld seemed to move thatway some years ago.”

For 18 months, Luhrmann had an office in a barn that housed the Presley archives at Graceland, Memphis, as he researched the film, the dreaming-and-discovery stage that he loves most. “The way I make movies is I live them,” he says. “If I could, I’d probably just research them and live them and never make them, because production’s hard.”

His long sojourn back home in Australia has helped him understand why. “I’ve only just come to realise that if I was anything when I was young, I was a fan,” he says. “Being a kid from the country, and so devoted to music and films,was probablywhat droveme onmy road.”He sees that “unbridled enthusiasm” as part ofwhat fuels the flashes of lightning that illuminate our landscape – and just sometimes the world. “I was born in a small town in the middle of nowhere. Herons Creek had seven houses and three of them didn’t have anyone in them,” he says. “There’s something of the Australian ethos in that: we do look to the rest of the world. We do have an outward-looking energy, I think, in general.”

It’s easy to be swept into that energy as he speaks. Even before he was a director, Luhrmann trained as an actor.

If Faisal’s Tent is a very consciously constructed theatre, the story Luhrmann tells there is every bit a performance.

No accident that accommodation and transportation are secondary in the Bazmark philosophy. Both serve communication.

And hair. Luhrmann was born Mark Anthony Luhrmann, a Shakespearean moniker he changed to “Bazmark” by deed poll in his teens. The new name elided his Christian and nickname, short for “Basil Brush”, a reference to the unruly afro he wore at the time. What is gobsmacking about the story,whichcomestowards the topofLuhrmann’sWikipedia page, is the precocious sense of self-invention, not tomention manifest destiny, it suggests in a kid still at high school. Of course, Mark is also a homonym for marque, or brand, and it is under the Bazmark flag that the extraordinary caravan of Luhrmann’s subsequent career has travelled down the decades, through studios, cities and genres, from movies to TV, ads, and record and design projects. “I’m like a carny ... and this is a circus,” he says at one point, referring to his latest camp. “But a circus as run by an army ... I always say this is not a job, it’s a life. You’re either circus or you’re not.”

Not unlike life within the original Moulin Rouge, founded in the 19th century by another self-invented impresario, France’s own P.T. Barnum, Charles Zidler, onto which Luhrmann grafted everything from Puccini’s La Bohème and Verdi’s La Traviata to contemporary pop music and Hollywood musicals. Luhrmann was asked recently which of Moulin’s protagonists he most resembled, which got him thinking. “I mean I relate a lot to Zidler, because he’s got this great big carnival of extraordinary characters that he brings together to put on a show,” hemuses. “But I also feel a lot like Christian [the young writer played by Ewan McGregor who competes for Satine, Nicole Kidman’s doomed courtesan/ star] in that he was a young man on an Orphean journey, always trying to tell his story and his life is the story.

“Then again, I sometimes feel equally like Satine. Her life, her relationships are all wrapped up in the creative reality she lives. She’s someone who is trapped by the special qualities she brings to that place. In the end, Satine cannot escape the Moulin Rouge.” •

Screen Australia CEO Graeme Mason agrees: “We have an enormous opportunity, but it’s up to us to build on the fact that everyone has discovered us,” he says. “We’re Englishspeaking, we’re a safe location, and we’re a location most people want to go to once. Once they come down here they find our crews and facilities are amazing. And how integrated we already are into Hollywood.”

To Luhrmann, the real risk is that we won’t make the most of our current advantage. Australia’s cultural development has always been fitful, he says, characterised by breakthrough moments of vision, purple patches of support for culture that tend to dissipate into longueurs of inaction.

“There is a particular Aussie creativity that I refer to as ‘flashes of lightning’,” he says. “I mean, look at the Sydney skyline, pretty generic and then boom, flash of lightning, the Opera House.Where did that come from?” Luhrmann and Martin were themselves the product of such a moment. Their breakthrough 1990 Opera Australia production of La Bohème came in the same year the Hawke government, having boosted arts funding 40 per cent in three years, took direct funding control and gave it an extra $1 million. The couple were swept into a moment of cultural priority and confidence, like Barrie Kosky, who would go on to become a star opera director. “We were doing radical operas here, us and Barrie,” Luhrmann says. “Because the arts were really well-funded and supported, and we were really into it.”

That experimentation in turn helped fuel international revolutions in not just opera but film. Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet applied the same luridly contemporising approach to the Bard. And you can trace the shadow of La Bohème’s “L’amour” sign, inspired by the Coke sign in Sydney’s Kings Cross, throughout Luhrmann’s career, from Moulin Rouge! to his 2004 ad for Chanel No.5. Not to mention the influence of opera’s fundamental grounding in music as the engine of drama.

The love sign would be echoed too in the 1993 campaign launch that Luhrmann – freshly famous from 1992’s Strictly Ballroom – stage-managed for Paul Keating, the word AUSTRALIA emblazoned across a cobalt curtain.

In the wake of Keating’s unlikely “true believers” victory, Luhrmann lobbied the PM for a city film studio in Sydney.

“I said: Look, very few cities in the world have a studio right in the middle of the city,” he recalls. “You don’t know what that means to filmmaking.” Fox would be announced a year later as part ofAustralia’s first major cultural policy, the fouryear, $250 million Creative Nation strategy, which Keating hoped would draw a line under “our post-colonial era” and say “goodbye to it”.

“I always felt that Australia would have its very particular moment,”Luhrmannsays. “Which iswhy Iwas so passionate about becoming a republic. People think that’s just a symbol but it’s not. Surely we’re mature enough to elect our head of state?” It’s that sort of maturity that is on offer – but also required – now, he says. “It has to stop being flashes of lightning. There needs to be consistent, concerted policy and incentives but also consistent infrastructure.”

It’s the sort of strategic, long-term thought and investment for which George Miller has been calling for a decade now, not just to maximise the economic impact of films made here, but also to give the talent Australia mints and exports a long-term, stable home base from which to work. And the day after the Financial Review speaks to Luhrmann, another Australian star, Russell Crowe, does something about it, announcing he’s backing a $438 million fully integrated feature-film production and post-production complex down the road from the Goldie in Coffs Harbour, another town built, LA-like, around a highway.

“Whatever your thoughts on a higher power, they’re a great stage manager, a great writer,” Luhrmann says. We’re discussing his personal revolution of the past 18 months. “I mean, you couldn’t write this. Just when I think I’ve seen or experienced it all, I end up making a film about Elvis by myself on the Gold Coast – and being wowed by it.

It’s energised, enlivenedme to findmyself atmy age back in a place not unlikewhere Igrewup,”he says. “I really surf change ... the energy never scares me. I love to be lifted up by it.”

In many ways the Gold Coast has been eerily familiar.

Not only is it a few hours’ drive from Herons Creek, but the couple have found the maximalist fabrics, wallpapers and rugs Martin began designing more than a decade ago for retail are everywhere, as if she’d already art-directed it.

But then 2021 has been a year of milestones: a quarter of a century since Romeo + Juliet,which divided critics but is now regarded as a milestone adaptation; 20 years since Moulin Rouge! single-handedly revived the fortunes of the movie musical, an artform Luhrmann had been warned was dead.

And by the time Elvis makes it to cinemas in 2022, Strictly Ballroom, his first film, made at just 29, will turn 30. Does he feel vindicated? “I’m much more focused on what’s in front of me,” he says. “Letme tell you, as soon as you get towhere I am, you forget about it. I feelmuseummoments occasionally, but honestly, inmy soul, I feel like I’mjust getting going and haven’t donemuch yet.”

Luhrmann did though recently revisit the problem child of his oeuvre, 2008’s Australia, working with Hulu on an asyet unannounced long-play version titled Faraway Downs, which he says will tease out some of the larger themes the film couldn’t. Whatever Australia’s merits – and he’s frank it “really didn’t land in the US” where it matters – he always intended the film tomake a statement not just about, but to, this country. “I’mnot saying thatAustralia or FarawayDowns are in themselves the singular gesture of self-reflection or a maturing attitude,” he says. “But I didwant to take [on] some of the more difficult issues and realities of our history, and in a broad way that allowed as many people into it as possible, rather than a film that would be seen by a very limited audience.”

In the same way he took on Elvis, he says, not so much for the singer as the times he sang. “When I look at musical biography, it’s not really about the life,”he says. “I’mnot about lionising Elvis. I just saw him as the best canvas on which to explore America in the modern age, the ’50s, ’60s and ’70s.” The engine of that drama, he says, is the relationship between an artist who spanned genres, eras and races, and the P.T. Barnum character of Colonel TomParker, the former circus carny who made and then ruined him.

“I saw this story of the Colonel and Elvis as a really great prism through which to explore the latter part of the 20th century,” Luhrmann says. “Elvis represents what happens when a kid lives in one of four designated white houses in a black community. Something new comes about, a fusion between country and African-American music, gospel and country-and-western music.TheColonel represents that other quality in America, ‘the big sell’. The tension between the two is great when they’re in balance. But when they’re thrown out of balance, and it just becomes about exploiting and selling and ceases to be creative, then the world’s out of whack ... and theworld seemed to move thatway some years ago.”

For 18 months, Luhrmann had an office in a barn that housed the Presley archives at Graceland, Memphis, as he researched the film, the dreaming-and-discovery stage that he loves most. “The way I make movies is I live them,” he says. “If I could, I’d probably just research them and live them and never make them, because production’s hard.”

His long sojourn back home in Australia has helped him understand why. “I’ve only just come to realise that if I was anything when I was young, I was a fan,” he says. “Being a kid from the country, and so devoted to music and films,was probablywhat droveme onmy road.”He sees that “unbridled enthusiasm” as part ofwhat fuels the flashes of lightning that illuminate our landscape – and just sometimes the world. “I was born in a small town in the middle of nowhere. Herons Creek had seven houses and three of them didn’t have anyone in them,” he says. “There’s something of the Australian ethos in that: we do look to the rest of the world. We do have an outward-looking energy, I think, in general.”

It’s easy to be swept into that energy as he speaks. Even before he was a director, Luhrmann trained as an actor.

If Faisal’s Tent is a very consciously constructed theatre, the story Luhrmann tells there is every bit a performance.

No accident that accommodation and transportation are secondary in the Bazmark philosophy. Both serve communication.

And hair. Luhrmann was born Mark Anthony Luhrmann, a Shakespearean moniker he changed to “Bazmark” by deed poll in his teens. The new name elided his Christian and nickname, short for “Basil Brush”, a reference to the unruly afro he wore at the time. What is gobsmacking about the story,whichcomestowards the topofLuhrmann’sWikipedia page, is the precocious sense of self-invention, not tomention manifest destiny, it suggests in a kid still at high school. Of course, Mark is also a homonym for marque, or brand, and it is under the Bazmark flag that the extraordinary caravan of Luhrmann’s subsequent career has travelled down the decades, through studios, cities and genres, from movies to TV, ads, and record and design projects. “I’m like a carny ... and this is a circus,” he says at one point, referring to his latest camp. “But a circus as run by an army ... I always say this is not a job, it’s a life. You’re either circus or you’re not.”

Not unlike life within the original Moulin Rouge, founded in the 19th century by another self-invented impresario, France’s own P.T. Barnum, Charles Zidler, onto which Luhrmann grafted everything from Puccini’s La Bohème and Verdi’s La Traviata to contemporary pop music and Hollywood musicals. Luhrmann was asked recently which of Moulin’s protagonists he most resembled, which got him thinking. “I mean I relate a lot to Zidler, because he’s got this great big carnival of extraordinary characters that he brings together to put on a show,” hemuses. “But I also feel a lot like Christian [the young writer played by Ewan McGregor who competes for Satine, Nicole Kidman’s doomed courtesan/ star] in that he was a young man on an Orphean journey, always trying to tell his story and his life is the story.

“Then again, I sometimes feel equally like Satine. Her life, her relationships are all wrapped up in the creative reality she lives. She’s someone who is trapped by the special qualities she brings to that place. In the end, Satine cannot escape the Moulin Rouge.” •

HEADLINE: Conviction politician
TEXT:
John Howard’s brand of social conservatism and economic liberalism won him four terms as prime minister. Relaxed and comfortable about his legacy, he worries there is no blueprint for the geopolitical and economic challenges ahead.

“Not bad, is it?” says John Howard as I stand gaping at the sweeping view from his retirement perch, high up in the Sydney skyline. “John Faulkner got me this. It’s better than the office I had when I was primeminister.”

We are standing admiring the panorama –which stretches from the Harbour Bridge to the Pacific Ocean to the southern beaches – visible fromHoward’s 53rd-storey official ex-prime ministerial office. The rooms were provided to him by the Rudd government after he lost the 2007 election. Faulkner was the minister responsible for Commonwealth properties and, given the loathing of Labor supporters for Howard as prime minister, itwas a magnanimous gesture.

I am meeting Howard to interview him for the first time in more than 20 years, to talk about the long story of Australia’s political, economic and social evolution over the 70-year lifespan of The Australian Financial Review – 70 years that covered pretty neatly John Howard’s life in politics. It’s arguable that no othernameappeared more often in Financial Review print than John Howard’s.

Now out of Parliament for 14 years and in his early 80s, Howard’s interest in politics remains intense; he still keeps engaged. “I don’t call members of the government – unless I feel very strongly about something. I think they are entitled to make their own luck ... and also to make their own mistakes.”

But they do call him.

Prime Minister Scott Morrison calls “for a chat” every couple of weeks. Defence Minister Peter Dutton and Howard talk “quite a bit”.

And Federal Treasurer Josh Frydenberg called him several times as hewas thinking through this year’s federal budget – with its huge increase in the deficit and its forecast of an unprecedented increase in debt.

“Josh spoke to me on several occasions to outline what he was proposing to do,” says Howard. “And I agreed with it. But I said to him: “If you announce exit dates, you have got to stick to them.”

As Howard wistfully surveys the breathtaking view from his official office, it occurs to me that what he sees each day that he comes to work – he plays golf on Mondays – is not just scenery but a panorama of a people and a nation that he has played a significant personal role in shaping.

Howard melded social conservatism and economic liberalism into a political product that he used to market himself as a “conviction politician”. It propelled him from someone who seemed destined to be an also-ran into a fourterm prime ministership.

I know the Howard story well. He was a permanent feature of my career covering politics.

Seeing him again after all these years – frailer, with his tonsure-like baldness having pushed his hairline to the lower reaches of his scalp and with his grey, bushy eyebrows defining his face – I am given the strong impression that Howard lives with the deep satisfaction that he made his own luck. By sheer doggedness and determination, he achieved his ambition to become prime minister and make his mark on Australia.

And he did that in spades, halting and turning back Paul Keating’s march towards a progressive Australian republic. Long regarded as colourless andboring,Howardhasbecomeoneof the Liberal party’s greatest weapons on the campaign front.

He’s even popular with the younger generation, who never knew him in office, and who admire him for his stance on gun control.

But as relaxed and comfortable as he obviously is about his own political story, Howard is not so comfortable about where the bigger story for Australia may be headed.

He worries about a future course – for the economy and for Australia’s geopolitical challenges – for which there are few guideposts. Asked if he is apprehensive, he says: “Well, in an inquiring way.

“None of us alive today has lived through such lowinterest rates and such high debt.We are in uncharted territory. But if you print money, you borrow too much, you increase public sector borrowing, it places tensions on interest rates.

“It’s an issue. Since the ’70s nothing was considered to be more important than controlling spending and balancing the budget. The debt levels we now see will have to come down. Thatwill be a huge challenge. I don’tpretend toknow the answer to it. I don’t think anybody does.”

And then there’s our largest trading partner. “The relationship with China is the biggest foreign policy and economic issue that we have faced in livingmemory.” Nevertheless, Howard feels at ease with the way his successors on the conservative side of politics have managed his legacy. He has high regard for Scott Morrison, a leader after his own heart – or at least, of his own method of leadership.

Howard stands accused by his adversaries of being a divisive leader and as having created the politics which has left a legacy of bitter partisanship. But he is unfazed and doesn’t accept this description of the state of politics. “Actually, I think things were more polarised in the decades of the ’50s, ’60s and ’70s. The ideological divide was very deep, overhung by the Vietnam War, the sacking of the Whitlam government. There was deep partisanship then. I don’t think the debates are as bitter now. The expression I would use to describe the state of politics now is ‘fragmented’.”

Howard says that fragmentation is apparent in the growth in the numbers on the crossbenches in Parliament which “is a thoroughly bad development”. He says it reflects the collapse of political party membership and the decline of political parties being organisations that represent broad-based community interests.

“The language of factions has entered the culture of the Liberal Party much more strongly than it used to. I think it is just amajor trend in all political parties. People don’t join organisations theway they used to. As a result, political parties’ rank and file membership is less representative of the people who normally vote for them. So the potential for control by groups or factions is greater. Social media has reinforced our alienation from groups. It is a very different political culture.” As Howard reflects on the past 70 years of Australian political history, he talks about, essentially, four distinct phases.

The first was the post-war Menzies era when thepolitical contestwas fundamentally about foreign policy, national security and defence. Thesewere the issues that drewHoward into politics. His early political speeches were in defence ofAustralia’s involvement in theVietnam War. The post-war European migration (“one of the great achievements of Australia”), the boom years that saw home ownership rise to the highest rate in the world and virtually full employment meant that there was little argument over economic policy in the Menzies years. “There was really a consensus that we were doing OK as we were,” Howard says.

The second phase saw the shift from politics dominated by foreign affairs and security to politics dominated by economics.

With the oil shock of the early ’70s, the surge in inflation that followed, the end of the Vietnam War and the beginning of large-scale Asian migration – and with regional economies modernising and putting growing pressure on Australia’s protected and heavily regulated economy – the political system failed to cope.

The Whitlam Labor government, which came to power promising to transform Australia, was overwhelmed by the new challenges, leading to the 1975 constitutional crisis. But the Fraser government that followed failed to respond to the demands that the changing world was throwing at Australia.

“We were complacent,” says Howard. “I mean, the world was changing and we weren’t.

I think the reason change didn’t occur is that the dominant influences were, still, that the old approach would do the job, provided we were careful about spending. That was wrong.”

Howard admits that until he became federal Treasurer in 1977, when he was 38 years of age, he had little appreciation of the compelling need for liberalising economic reform. “Look, I was anything but a paid-up free marketeer when I became Treasurer. I sort of saw it very much in terms of balancing the books. But the more I sawwhatwas happening from that position –we were spinning wheels – the more I realised how important economic reform was.”

Howard credits the federal Treasury, his then senior economic adviser, John Hewson, and the Financial Review for heavily influencing his views on reform.

“I often reflect on that period and, I mean, Max Walsh [Financial Review editor and managing editor between 1974 and 1981]was very influential as an economic thinker.Walsh had a great influence in consolidating the complete link between economicmanagement and politics.”

The Fraser government’s failure to confront the reform challenges after what Howard calls “the economic disaster of the Whitlam government”, compounded the crisis.

They were not confronted until the election of the Hawke government in 1983 – the beginning of the next phase of the Australian political story.

While Howard concedes that the Coalition’s long, historic political dominance had been, in significant part, helped by Labor’s divisions and failures, he does acknowledge the Labor years ofHawke andKeating –duringwhich he suffered bitter personal setbacks – as a historically important period for the Australian economy.

Howard says there is no doubt the single biggest and the most important economic reform of that whole period was the floating of the dollar. “Thatmarked a generational change in attitudes to economic reform in Australia,” Howard says.

The Hawke-Keating reform agenda – floating the currency, financial deregulation and opening of foreign banks, privatisation, tariff reductions and the beginnings of freeing the labour market – had been transformative. And, he said, it had happened because of the bipartisanship that he had given for the reforms, against resistance from within the coalition. “I note that Labor didn’t extend the same bipartisanship tomy reform agenda,” Howard says.

The momentum of reform did continue into the Howard years. There was the curtailing of the power of the Maritime Union of Australia on the waterfront, independence for the Reserve Bank and the politically risky goods and services tax. And there was Work Choices, Howard’s bold package of labour market changes that were deeply unpopular and repealed by the Rudd government after Howard’s 2007 election loss.

But by the time of Howard’s election in 1996, reform fatigue was setting in. This marked the beginning of the next phase of the Australian political story – and it can accurately be termed the age of John Howard. Just as Menzies dominated post-war Australia and the Hawke- Keating partnership dominated economic reform, Howard’s brand of economically liberal-socially conservative politics has dominated Australia since the mid-1990s.

Howard says the times ended up suiting him because: “There was a sense developing in society that too much was changing and that there was a need to give people a bit of reassurance.”

Howardism (definedmore by his uncompromising assault on political correctness than by his economic philosophy) firstemergedwith his controversial 1988OneAustraliapolicy statement in which he walked away from bipartisanship on immigration, multiculturalism and Indigenous policy.

It was a stumbling start: Howard tripped himself up with his comments about the need to slow Asian immigration – which he now says “was not expressed with the most judicious choice of words”.

The storm this unleashed defined Howard – for many Australians on the progressive side of politics – as a divisive leader, willing to tap into the darker side of Australia’s historical struggle with race issues.

But despite that furore, Howard didn’t flinch. Nor has he since, all these years later making it clear he believes that, at the time, there really was a threat to the nation’s social cohesion. He followed up a few months after One Australia with his Future Directions manifesto – released at the end of 1988, wrapped in images of a family in front of their whitepicket- fenced house and ridiculed by Labor as looking to the past rather than the future. “It tapped directly into the sense that too much of the old Australia and its values was being lost as economic reformmorphed into rapid social change,” Howard says.

Even though Howard subsequently lost the Liberal leadership to Andrew Peacock, Future Directions remained on the table as the Howard manifesto, with its set of economically liberal and socially conservative ideals and policies. It was resurrected when Howard stunningly returned to the leadership ahead of the 1996 election.

“We did tap into something then,” Howard says. “It anticipated the debate that would occur over the next 20 to 30 years.We are still in this debate now about how we value the established values and traditions of our society. I think the white picket fence was something that, silently, people actually wanted.”

Looking back over the past seven decades, Howard says there has been an extraordinary transformation of the country, in which immigration – the post-war wave  of European immigrants and the more recent Asian immigration – has been hugely significant.

“But it, sort of, hasn’t in anyway, inmy opinion, obliterated the old Australia. Migration changed Australia but didn’t change it beyond recognition.”

Asked about how he sees his own legacy, he says: “The thing was, I did not submit to the view that if you were an economic liberal you had to be a social liberal. I was an economic liberal but I also had strong, socially conservative values.

“At a time of incredible turmoil around the world brought about by things like rapid change and terrorism, I preserved and really reinforced the social cohesion of the country. I preserved the strengths and size of the middle class, which is the most precious asset we have.”

Howard maintains his vigilance over what he originally termed “political correctness” and now adopts the contemporary description of “wokeism”. “There are certain things I’d like to see [the government do] ... I mean, I’d like, every so often, to see a strong attack on culturalwokeism.” A particular target for Howard’s ongoing fight against political correctness is businesses that he accuses of engaging in “virtue signalling” in their corporate decision-making.

“Obviously, individuals who run companies are entitled to views that amount to what is loosely called virtue signalling.

But I just don’t know how a corporation can seriously say it supports this or that, on what are totally social issues.”

He baulks at this being described as “cultural wars”. That said, Howard has a wide definition of what comes into this category: to him it includes the battle of climate change policy.

“I’m not a believer,” says Howard when I ask if there is a danger that Australia could – like in the ’60s and ’70s – be left behind on reform to deal with challenges posed by global warming. “I guess there is a risk, yes. But I can’t feel terribly anxious about it. Not the way I did about the compelling reforms of the early 1980s. It was easy to be a believer about those things.”

On any list of the reform challenges facing Australia, he would put climate change-linked policy well down that list.

“The most important thing on climate change is to hold the party together. I mean, I thought Malcolm Turnbull presented very well after he became leader. But he didn’t understand – and this is something I told him – on climate change the most important thing you’ve got to do is hold the party together.” Howard thinks Scott Morrison gets this.

Howard’s “to-do list” of economic reforms continues to be topped by the reforms he attempted to tackle in government but never completed – deregulation of labour markets and tax reform. But he does not feel the sense of urgency about big economic reforms that he did in the 1980s.

“It is a different world now,” he says, arguing that the challenge ahead now for government and policymakers is how to come out of the unprecedented, COVID-19-induced monetary and fiscal policy settings.

This marks the fourth phase of the story as seen through John Howard’s eyes.

The response of governments to the pandemic – locking down their economies to stop the spread of the virus, and then pumping in huge amounts of money, has created a completely new set of challenges.

“But you have to say it hasworked,” he says, referring to the massive government spending around theworld. “And if you adopt the Latin maxim – res ipsa loquitur [the facts speak for themselves] – that’s obvious. What I do believe is that there is going, ultimately, to be a need to return to balance. That is going to be a huge challenge.”

While Howard has concerns about how that will be achieved, an immediate issue worries him more. In fact, he ranks it at the top of his list of challenges.

“The relationship with China is the biggest foreign policy and economic issue that we have faced in living memory. I mean, we must never forget how important China is to us economically.We would be crazy to forget that.

“Having said that, theymust still see us as a very important economic partner. They want our coal still. They want our iron ore. And, I think, some of the trade diversion in the nonfossil fuel area that’s occurred over the last year indicates that they cannot be too cavalier. They have chosen fairly strategically.

“Now having said that, I’m dead against any gratuitous differences.”

Asked if he had heard “the drums ofwar” beating, to quote Home Affairs Department SecretaryMike Pezzullo, Howard says: “Well, I just think you have to be careful with words. I mean, the personwho said that is a very good public servant.

But that didn’t help.”

Howard says he would not have done anything radically different from the way the Morrison government has handled the crisis. “There is no magic bullet, no secret emissaries. That is not going to work because this is quite a decisive shift. You just need to take the opportunities you can to manage this.”

He adds: “I am a huge optimist about Australia.”

As he gazes out from his Sydney loft, Howard sees in today’s Australia the nation he described in his preelection “headland” speeches as the one he wanted it to be: prosperous and comfortably conservative, shaped in his own vision. •

HEADLINE: Repointing the raft
TEXT:
His combative edge has been softened, just a touch. But Paul Keating, who drove the great economic reforms of a generation ago, has lost none of his passion

“I could have been with my father’s business, the junior Chamber of Commerce and the Jaycees Club. I didn’t have to happen. But I did happen.” It’s Paul Keating speaking and the “happen” part relates to his role in the ’80s-’90s transformation of the Australian economy from sclerotic to supple.

“I said over and over in the House of Representatives, as prime minister, as treasurer, and in interviews with the media, that I had given the country a new economic engine.

The job I had was to repoint the raft at opportunity – to fifi nd our security in Asia, and not from Asia.”

Doing so again in 2021 is a big ask. The world is racked by the contagion, and we live in a region of increasing tension.

A resurgent China is challenging the US-mandated postwar order, and is intent on punishing Australia for being too uppity. Meanwhile, Australia will struggle to repay its COVID-19-generated debt for at least 40 years unless it improves its economic performance.

Keating believes a “new philosophy of leadership” – in reality, an updated version of his crash-through style – is required to give Australia a good future. By adopting this new leadership style, he argues we can have it all – a strong relationship with China, continuation of the American alliance, and the confifi dence to improve our economic performance.

The former prime minister (1991-1996), treasurer (1983- 1991), and self-described “big-picture man” swats away questions about details, but says if Australia pursues the right approach, the will to embrace reform will emerge.

“Anyone who’s had to make changes requires a new philosophy of leadership. The old philosophy where we didn’t do good policy denied the benefifi ts we were entitled to. Under this new philosophy of leadership you proselytise good policy, you educate the country to good policy. The good thing about proselytising for good policy is that by educating the country into the reasons for good policy, and being marked up by the country, [you] bring the country forward.”

What Keating calls a focus group approach means “people get fed their own received wisdom”. The drift of his argument is that leadership, or the lack of it, is a bipartisan malaise, although there was no criticism of ALP leader Anthony Albanese in any of his comments.

Paul Keating is speaking to the Financial Review in his commodious offifi ce suite in Potts Point, Sydney. The building – Tusculum – is named after a ruined ancient Roman city.

Keating holds meetings and reads documents amid his extensive collection of statues, paintings and ornaments, or what conservative commentator Paddy McGuinness once airily dismissed as “bric-a-brac”.

Outside, COVID-19’s dark shadow is reappearing once again in the Emerald City, as a confusing miasma of lockdowns, partial shutdowns and border closures spread across Australia.

Between interviews, global tensions also rise. Just before our second talk, the G7 meets in Cornwall, on England’s south-west coast, along with the leaders of India, South Korea, South Africa and Australia, and calls for a resolute approach by democracies towards China. It is pretty much the same mood at a NATO summit a few days later, and in bilateral meetings Prime Minister Scott Morrison has with his UK counterpart, Boris Johnson, and French President Emmanuel Macron.

Keating is not impressed with Morrison’s effort. “Two hundred and thirty-three years after the British landing [in Botany Bay], we fifi nd ourselves returning to Britain to fifi nd our security in Asia. I believe we should fifi nd our security in Asia.

We are not going to fifi nd our security in Cornwall in Britain.”

At this juncture, it’s relevant to point out that Keating’s street cred rests on the fact that he has been a standout in giving Australia an economic future, and in the process enhancing our security in the region. Back in the ’80s, a time when Singapore strongman Lee Kuan Yew was warning that Australians could end up as “the poor white trash of  Asia”, Keating jointly presided over the opening up of the Australian economy.

The other key figure in this generation-ago reform program was Bob Hawke, Labor prime minister from 1983- 91. If Keating was the driver, Hawke was the enabler. In later years the two had a bitter falling-out. Keating bulldozed Hawke out of The Lodge and their unseemly verbal feud over who should take the most credit for Labor’s reform program continued for years after both retired from politics.

During our discussions, however, Keating’s rancour towards Hawke has gone. Mellow is not a word normally associated with theKeating persona, but some of the 77-yearold’s combative edge has been rounded out.

Keating retains considerable clout, however, as is attested by his recent successful public intervention supporting the continued graduated rise in compulsory superannuation.

There is also a Medici quality to his close involvement in Sydney planning issues, including the giant Barangaroo redevelopment on the north-western fringe of the city’s CBD.

The reforms of the ’80s and ’90s constitute the biggest redesign of the Australian economy since World War II, and arguably since the post-Federation Deakinite compact.

They include floating the dollar, deregulating the banks, allowing in foreign banks, cutting tariffs, reducing income tax, introducing dividend imputation, the fringe benefits Keating warns that without a “sensible economic policy then Australia is basically done for.

We will end up being a banana republic.”

1986 From the pages of history Keating’s ongoing influence in public life was evidenced by his recent push for compulsory superannuation increases.

tax and capital gains tax, enterprise bargaining, privatising Qantas, the Commonwealth Bank and CSL, compulsory superannuation and microeconomic reform. From here on in, let’s call them “The Change”.

Hawke, who died in 2019 on the eve of the May 18 federal election, established a unique connection with the electorate.Aformer Rhodes Scholar andACTUpresident, he understood how Australia worked, enjoyed good relations with business, and was committed, as his 1983 election slogan put it, to “bringing Australia together”.

Amid much media mocking, Hawke held a post-election national economic summit with business and the unions “to create a climate for common understanding of the scale and scope of Australia’s present crisis”. The facilitation process for The Change turned out to be the Hawke-negotiated government-union accord, where wage restraint was agreed in return for increases in the “social wage” such as tax cuts, the introduction of Medicare, and compulsory superannuation.

PaulKeating is hewn from different politicalwood.Hefirst left school at 14 (and later matriculated by attending night school), was a fierce factional warrior, and contemptuous of Labor-left followers, calling them “Balmain basket-weavers”.

There was little sign early on that he would drive the biggest post-warreformof theAustralianeconomy,onethat involved a radical departure from traditional Labor priorities because it was about growing the piemore than carving it up.

The significant policy-shaping experience for Keating was not engaging in proverbial ALP factional biffos, but as a teenager witnessing his father,Matt, engage in the thankless task of trying to persuade the English Scottish andAustralian Bank to grant a loan for his expanding engineering business.

Keating railed against the banks. “The monopoly given to Australia’s handful of private and public banks has produced the most conservative banking community in the world.

These hopeless institutions stand in the way of a growing level of Australian corporate ownership,” he told Parliament in September 1977. Two months later, the Financial Review editorialised that Keating’s view that local banks were “unresponsive to the challenges and rewards” in the mining industry “is a complaint that has considerable merit”.

Keating has kept the article in his clippings.

In 1981, The Sydney Morning Herald quoted Keating saying the ALP was full of people wanting to spend money.

“What’s wrong with trying to create it?” he asked at the time.

More pointed the following year, he told Labor luminary Bob Carr, who was then working for now-defunct magazine The Bulletin: “The political prizes in Australia will go to the party with the capacity to create new wealth.”

DuringthoseyearsKeatingspentmuchofhisparliamentary downtime talking with Max Walsh, the Financial Review’s political correspondent in Canberra, and later editor and managing editor. Colleagues recall Keating sitting in the one armchair in the AFR’s office in Old Parliament House, chewing the economic policy cud with Walsh, then the editorial benchmark for national political coverage.

“Super-bright, fast-talking, witty and gregarious, academically very raw but possessed of a driving ambition to succeed and willing to take risks to do so,” is the way Walsh once described an on-the-way-up Keating. “As Gough Whitlam once remarked, he was a throwback to the days when Labor was populated with bright, unqualified and unconnected young men who saw politics as their only way of making amark in the world.”

“Keating said I taught him economics,”Walsh said in 2013, on the eve of the 50th anniversary of the Financial Review as a national daily newspaper. “What I taught him is how important economics are, and he had the good fortune to have a terrific team at Treasury when he got there. David Morgan and Ted Evans were the important ones.

“He was very, very shaky at the beginning. Not surprising, of course – he was catapulted into the job [of shadow treasurer] just before the election. But his natural selfconfidence came through very quickly.”

Keating now says Walsh was mainly helpful in pointing out where the power lay in Treasury. “I had the helpers – a little bit of analytics on the way which helped you round out the economics,” Keating says. “[But] there was no consensus framework in the bureaucracy – in the Treasury, Finance Department, or the big operating departments. If I hadn’t had a view about how the market economy should operate, these changes would not have happened. If I had relied on the Treasury, the IAC or the Reserve Bank, these changes would not have happened.

“It was like a code. You had to see the pieces for what they were.Youhadto get thepolicy pieces together toget it right.”An “incremental” approach meant underwhelming results. “The reformation of theAustralian economywas delivered radically.

“When I was sworn in as treasurer, I realised that the whole economic framework of Australia was protectionist, defensive and self-defeating. After the bout of inflation in the 1970s, when the convertibility of dollars for gold under the BrettonWoods arrangements had been revoked by [then US President] Richard Nixon, it was a case of ‘every man, or country, for himself’ as currencies floated against each other in a quest for competitiveness. Countries that had [fixed] exchange rates and wage-cum-productivity systems out of line were in need of remedial policy to keep up with the pack. Australia, like a bunny in the headlights,was caught in a near-terminal bout of stagflation.

“Every important price in the economy was set on the cabinet table – the rates of exchange, the rates of interest, wage rates through centralised wage fixing, prices through tariffs. And a tax system which taxed income too heavily – leaving capital profits free, while taxing equity twice. As our terms of trade deteriorated and competitiveness slipped, we relied more and more on overseas savings, with the current account deficit ratcheting up to fund ourselves.

“The whole economic framework was insular, introspective and regressive. Neither the bureaucracy nor the polity had a remedy for it. There was no consensus between the political parties, nor was there a consensual framework within the bureaucracy.

“Somesectionsofthebureaucracyhadideas,eachgenerally unconnected from the other, while cabinets and economic ministers lacked any insight, let alone an ability to construct a reform agenda. The only hope of remedy lay in a radical reformation of policy, not an acceleration in incrementalism.

This required a new philosophy of leadership.”

The Change was a tough grind over 13 years, from 1983- 1996. It was a tall order for a Labor government but it was backed by voters. The ALP’s reform administration won five elections – four by Hawke and one by Keating. For a Labor Party which has been in office in Canberra for just one-third of the 120 years of Federation, it was a unique electoral achievement. In terms of longevity, the Hawke- Keating era has only been bested by the Hughes-Bruce non- Labor government and Robert Menzies’ standout record of winning seven elections in a row.

Moreover, the Hawke-Keating period in office was achieved despite a balance of payments crisis in 1986-87 – one marked by Keating’s dramatic warning that Australia could become a “banana republic”. Therewas also the brutal 1990-91 downturn, or, to again borrowKeating’s phraseology, the recession “we had to have”.

On the other side, The Change threw into sharp relief a tension gnawing away at the Liberal Party between being a self-proclaimed “free enterprise” party and a status quo political grouping. Nick Greiner, the reforming Liberal premier of NSW (1988-1992), one-time Liberal Party president, and current Australian consul-general in New York, has rationalised Labor’s ’80s-90s economic reforms as picking “low-hanging fruit”. If this was the case, why wasn’t the same pro-market “low-hanging fruit” picked earlier by Coalition governments?

It was a long, exhausting struggle for Keating, but the rewards finally came. From the early ’90s, or just over halfway through Labor’s reform program, productivity started to take off, and the best years were the decade from the early ’90s to the early noughties. In the 15-year period up to 2005, productivity grew 37 per cent; in the 15-year period following that, productivity increased by just 17 per cent. Another way of looking at it is that while for the past 30 years up to the COVID-19 outbreak productivity growth averaged 1.5 per cent a year, it has been below 0.5 per cent for the past five years. The Change, Keating says, was in “the general suppleness and flexibility of the economy: a floating exchange ratewhich takes the external shocks, the openness of product markets whichmeans any deflation around theworld is enjoyed here; and a sensible tax system which taxes capital profits and [removes] the double tax on equity”.

Since the dollar float, exchange rate movements have acted “as a buffer against an inflationary surge coming from a rapid increase in national income. The economy will bend in the wind. The dollar went down to 48¢ [against the US dollar] during the Asian financial crisis [in 1997-98], so you got twoAustralian dollars for every one US dollar. This saved the country and saved businesses.

“It was the most flexible economy in the Western world and this was proved by the fact that for 30 years, short of six months, this economy had no negative [growth] because the flexible economy was so sound.We eschewed protectionism wherein I dismantled the whole Deakinite edifice.”

I ask Keating about the role of global media magnate Rupert Murdoch in influencing Labor policy, but he is dismissive. “In terms of economic impact, Murdoch had no economic impact.” Since that period Murdoch has become “more conservative andmore right-wing. I don’twant to talk about him. TheFinancial Review has had a bigger impact on policy than all the News Ltd papers [put] together.”

Keating also contrasts his achievements with those of his successor, John Howard, the political Lazarus who thrashed Keating in the 1996 election, won another three elections, and held office for 11½ years. Apart from the GST – “amodest tax change” (although one which Keating tried and failed to introduce) – “there were no structural reforms undertaken by the Howard government”. The Howard-Costello government did, however, grant the RBA full independence and extinguished Australia’s public debt.

This Keating narrative on the 24½ years of the Hawke- Keating-Howard governments is not received wisdom in some quarters. Kicking contrary views into touch, he forgoes his usual combination of dockside argot and compelling word pictures, saying “most journalists in Canberra know that their supervisors won’t like it if they don’t mention the Liberal Party. They tap them in.

“Howard said ‘I was there supporting the changes.’ His real record is that he opposed the fringe benefits tax and the capital gains tax, which were introduced to broaden the tax base and at the same time reduce the top income tax rate from 60¢ in the dollar to 47¢ .

“How then do you think we could lower the income tax rate from 60 to 49 and then 47? You [Howard] didn’t put your hand up to facilitate the changes to the tax system by the taxation of capital gains and the taxation of fringe benefits. In the 11½ years they were in office, they brought it [the top income tax rate] down from 47 to 45. Howard and Costello brought it down by two percentage points. That’s how hopeless they were.

“There’s nothing to beat. No one did what we did.”

According to Keating, when John Howard was Treasurer in the Malcolm Fraser-led Coalition government in 1982, Howard visited the Treasury “to look at Statement Two” – essentially a budget-time exposition on the state of the economy. “John says: ‘how’s Statement Two coming along?’ [Treasury Department head John] Stone says: ‘Treasurer, you’ll be very pleased with that’.

“This is the time when the politicians didn’t run the country. They all just went around in their white cars.”

Keating himself prefers classic cars.

Like the great Japanese film Rashomon, different people have different recollections of the time, and of whom should take most of the credit. But Keating was the driver. •

HEADLINE: At last a prospectus for you
TEXT:
Having snared a position in this 70th anniversary magazine, Pierpont and his geriatric cronies figured that any reader who got this far would have his or her mental capabilities battered by all the fine writing before now. Their brain cells having been reduced by all that intellectual effort, some of them might just be in a condition where theywould be unable to resist subscribing to a prospectus for Trans Global Lithium Limited.

Like all prospectuses issued by Pierpont and his archaic colleagues, it is written to appeal to the currentmodish fashions. It offers, for a mere $2 a share, a lithiummine. The prospectus is a thin document, mostly writing about howlithium is the previously little-known metal that is now taking over the world.

Without actually saying so, the prospectus leaves readers with the impression that any reader who doesn’t have lithium already in their portfolio will be poorer as soon as the lithium boomreally gets into gear. As there are already a couple of dozen companies offering lithium to punters, Pierpont’s crew are hoping the chaps from the Australian Securities and Investments Commission don’t pay too much attention to this modest offering, which is seeking a mere $20 million from the unwary.

So send us a cheque and open a celebratory bottle of Bollinger, and don’t bother reading the rest of this column, which is devoted to a few dreary facts that may otherwise disturb your equanimity.

The lithium is a high-grade carbonate in Lac Alaotra in northern Madagascar.We like Madagascar because it sounds respectable.

Every Australian knows it’s a large island off the east cost of Africa, but nobody we know has ever been there.

The geologist’s report is from a firm in Sierra Leone.We found the firm’s name in a telephone book and ran off its heading on an old press we keep for such necessities. Our pet geologist Bottle wrote the report and our secretary Penwiper forged the signature of a partner in the Sierra Leone firm.

So we have a piece of paper from a firm of geologists who might even be respectable, saying the rock along the lake contains lithium averaging 4.27 per cent. That’s a very high lithium grade. Note that we have been very careful about ASIC’s travel budget. To obtain a conviction, one of its sleuths would have to fly to Madagascar and visit the lake and try to find some evidence that a geologist has been there too.

Then they would have to somehow get to Sierra Leone, find the geologist’s firm and get a statement from whoever was there that they’d never been to Madagascar and didn’t know anything about it.

And finally, they would have to prove that Pierpont and his mates knew the whole thing was bogus.

We would plead innocence and idiocy as well as hiring a good lawyer. At worst, we could flee the country or – being exceedingly prone to dementia – book into a good nursing home.

Ownership of the mine might also create a problem or two. The majority stake in Trans Global is held by a company in Venezuela. Upon reaching Venezuela, ASIC would find that company was actually owned by another in Ukraine, and all the shares in that one are owned by Pierpont and associates.

Distance would be a small problem for ASIC sleuths compared with other problems.

Madagascar is not too hard to reach, but Sierra Leone is a country which has been in political turmoil for decades. Venezuela (once oil-rich) does not now have an economy, having been wrecked by socialists. And Ukraine is likely to be invaded by Russia any day.

Finally, a word about lithium itself. One of the biggest markets for lithium has been for lithiumion batteries to be installed in modern vehicles, particularly cars. Lithium is the lightest metal known and has some peculiar properties, one of which being it is liable to catch fire.

Lithium-ion batteries are quite safe, although mobile phones using them have occasionally gone up in flames. So if your modern car is in a bad enough crash to break the battery casing, the battery may catch fire.

If it does, the best thing to do is run away. The batteries release a flammable vapour which is toxic and essentially provides its own fuel. So the fire does not go out by itself and can only be quelled by a specialist extinguisher.

Meanwhile, lithium being highly fashionable, we expect the prospectus to do well.

HEADLINE: Fortune favours reformers
TEXT:
Modest Member

TheModestMember was the nom de plume of South Australian federal Liberal MP Bert Kelly, under which he wrote a weekly column in the Financial Review from 1968 through to 1980. Kelly used his column to criticise protectionism and promote the benefits of free trade and competition. In so doinghe helpedpave theway for the reforms of the 1980s. The column below, written by a current federal LiberalMP, continues the tradition.

The Modest Member gave us at least two good lessons. The first was don’t let the National Party run your economic policy. The second was that political fortune favours the reformer.

Malcolm Fraser is remembered fondly for his social policy record on Vietnam and South Africa. But sadly, his economic policies now feature in textbooks as guidance in what to avoid. It could have been so different.

Fraser could have taken the advice of the original Modest Member, Bert Kelly, the swashbuckling MP for Wakefield from 1958-1977. He didn’t. Under too much influence from the National Party, Fraser pursued protectionism and subsidisation of industry. He avoided reform.

In the years that followed Fraser, it was proven that gutsy reforms could deliver electoral success. Floating the dollar, tax reform and even cutting tariffs resulted in the return of both the Hawke and Howard governments.

Howdo these two lessons play out today?

On the first lesson, keeping the National Party away from the key economic levers remains a high priority. This strategy works. For example, the trade portfolio has prospered under its first period of Liberal stewardship.

Long the domain of the Nationals, this portfolio has been held by a Liberal since 2013. Trade has seen its most successful period ever in terms of a record number of new agreements reached but also the breadth of the agreements. The recent agreements with Britain and Singapore have a digital economy focus which better reflects the modern services-based Australian economy.

There is no question that coal and iron ore are major sources of income for Australia, but they are no longer the great employers of Australians. Fewer than 40,000 people work in coal mining out of a labour market of 13 million. In total, mining employs fewer than 200,000 people. Their political influence is disproportionate.

More Australians work in the arts (210,000) than in mining. More than 1.2 million of us work in “professional, scientific and technical services”.

Mining and farming remain important to Australia. They are both highly organised and accustomed to political engagement, but they shouldn’t run policy on things like trade, tax and environment.

The targets we set for the Glasgow climate conference must be made for the economy today, not the economy of the McEwen age.

As for the second lesson, reform remains a political winner. No risk, no reward.

Having spent heavily to get Australia through the COVID-19 pandemic, we’ve saved today’s jobs, but haven’t done much for the jobs of the future. There has to be a renewed effort to drive productivity and new business investment.

We already know where the problems are. They live in the tax and the industrial relations systems. These are hard reform slogs but ultimately worth it as Hawke and Howard showed. And after spending more than $100 billion on JobKeeper, the most expensive program in history, the country must get a reform dividend.

Settling the squabbling within the federation has again shown itself to be a high priority. A state income tax should be part of the reform mix. It would stop the money-go-round and create a more competitive federation. The states should be forced to compete, otherwise what’s the point of a federation?Wemay as well have a unitary system.

The states should be forced to ask their citizens for money to spend on their constitutional obligations – rather than hide behind Canberra.

The blame game and buck-shifting that people have seen during the pandemic now gives the government a real set of reasons for moving on federation-driven reform. There should also be a simple set of workplace conditions to cover the whole economy, thereby doing away with the IR club’s darling, the “modern awards”. The pandemic created a reform narrative: the most complex and convoluted awards in retail and hospitality sectors were hit the hardest.

These ideas will be opposed by vested interests, namely big business and big government, which both did well out of the pandemic. Big business in conjunction with the big unions will oppose any IR changes, because the complex status quo keeps the employer groups and unions in business, literally.

Canberra’s deep state will resist any wearing down of the central government’s income tax power, as it has since World War II. The federal government’s income tax monopoly has been tightly protected by the deep state’s official family all these decades. Which is all the more reason to movenow, onthis and IR reform, given the once-in-a-century crisis that the pandemic poses.

Bert Kelly was forgotten by Malcolm Fraser but his legacy bloomed during the reform era which set up Australia for 30 years of growth: a world record. Long may we remember him and his lessons.

HEADLINE: Change of focus
TEXT:
of focus Top shots Photographs were few and far between in the early years of the Financial Review.

In the 1960s and 1970s, we were fond of running pictures of mines, ports and shopping centres. After an internal debate in the 1980s, we finally began capturing the people we wrote about. In more recent decades, our photos have become proof of this masthead’s pulling power.  This 1999 photo was the last taken of George Trumbull as CEO of AMP. “After the interview in his office was done, he showed me his memorabilia shelf and there was this native American headdress,” says Pamela Williams. “I asked him to put it on, and he did. It just looked so stunning. So I said ‘I would love to have a photo of you in that’.” When the photo ran on page one , it was just the thing to illustrate the story in which the American-born CEO lambasted “yellow-bellied Australian cowards” who, he said, were propagating lies about his bombastic remarks at a dinner with the PM.
