AMP’s chairman immediately wrote to Trumbull to tell him not to return to the office.

One of the very first actions taken by the Abbott government: posing for the cover of the 2013 Power issue of AFR Magazine.

It was taken in the Prime Minister’s office on the morning of September 20, shortly after the new PM and his ministers were sworn in by the Governor-General. “A lot of planning went into the shot,” said photographer Nic Walker. “Peta Credlin made some comment about it being try-hard Annie Leibovitz [the celebrated photographer at Vanity Fair]. I said if it was try-hard Leibovitz, we were doing it on one-hundredth of the budget.”

PLATINUM MAGAZINE 53 A year after inheriting his father’s empire, in 2006 James Packer finally succumbed to Pamela Williams’ and Damon Kitney’s requests for an interview. Alas, the photographer was 15 minutes late for the shoot. “It wasn’t his fault. But Packer was furious,” says Williams. “He said, ‘Right, you can have two minutes’.

When the photographer said he needed to set up all his lights, Packer replied, ‘Too bad, you’ve got two minutes’.” He smiled for a microsecond and the shot was taken. “It’s quite revelatory about Packer,” says Williams. “In his den, family pictures in frames. Focused, and annoyed.”

Kayla Itsines, photographed by Damian Bennett, on the cover of the 2018 Young Rich issue of AFR Magazine, presenting a new face to entrepreneurialism.

“Julie-anne Sprague, who had just been appointed as Rich List editor, had been using Itsines’ exercise workouts for years,” says AFR Magazine editor Matthew Drummond.

“Sprague suspected Itsines’ business was worth more than anyone realised, and did the maths. Three years later it sold for a reported $400 million.”

A handcuffed Rodney Adler is escorted into a corrective services van in 2005. He had just been sentenced to 4½ years’ prison over charges of dishonesty in relation to the $5.3 billion collapse of HIH Insurance. The photo was taken by Andrew Quilty who, with colleague Rob Homer, hired a ute and put a stepladder on the back. “That was the only way they could get sufficient height to get the shot,” says reporter Angus Grigg, who reported on the downfall of Adler. “The perp walk of white-collar criminals, we see that all the time in the US. But you rarely see it in Australia.”

Heather Ridout, in the 2008 Power issue, as chief executive of the Australian Industry Group. The Power issue is always a tough assignment for photographers, because the more powerful someone is, the less they want to reveal. “That’s the difficult thing with corporate types,” says Jessica Hromas, photo editor of the Financial Review at the time. “They are well schooled in the art of giving nothing away, in being as guarded as possible. In this shot, Andrew Quilty has captured that little magic moment of something else.”

HEADLINE: One of a kind
TEXT:
Within the span of just one generation, Frank Lowy migrated to Australia, revolutionised an industry, took his business to theworld and then sold it for $32 billion. One of Australia’s greatest-ever entrepreneurs, Lowy is keeping active in Israel, although he’s not entirely at peace.

Frank Lowy has always pushed himself and at 90, it’s no different. His day begins under a high-pressure shower of refrigerated water. Just before this bracing assault, he has swum a few laps, stretched and exercised as he watches the news on a big screen. Disciplines of a lifetime won’t allow him to linger in bed and an ambition to remain relevant drives him to get up early. But these days, there’s a new dimension to his routine.

As a boy, he watched his father pray every morning and nowhe too takes time to pause and do the same.At least once a month, his eldest son, David, flies himself fromNewYork to Israel to spend a week with his father. When possible, Peter comes from Los Angeles and Steven from Sydney.Whenever one of his sons is with him, they pray together and with this, a sense of tradition continues.

“When they are here, we’re up deep into the night, talking, reminiscing, planning and, of course, discussing business,” says Sir Frank, who was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II, at Windsor Castle in 2017. After breakfast overlooking the Mediterranean, he usually goes to his study where his workday begins. As his eyesight has weakened, he prefers that his secretary read him his emails. If she’s not there, he reads them himself, slowly.

The pandemic has all but grounded him in his multistorey home close to the Tel Aviv beachfront. He hasn’t been able to enjoy his new apartment overlooking Central Park in New York nor his much loved waterfront house in Sydney’s Point Piper, but has managed a few weeks in Greece on his immaculate 82-metre yacht.

His priorities have changed. Where once hewas possessed byWestfield, these days he rarely thinks of it. After devoting more than 60 years to building it into one of the largest retail property development companies in theworld,when he sold it in late 2017, he signed away his obsession.

“I felt huge relief, a tinge of sadness and recognised it was the end of an era, but also that I could look forward to being creative and involved in other things.”

Heand fellowEuropean emigre JohnSaunders had started out as partners in a delicatessen in 1955. The following year, they established the Westfield Building Company and four years later floated it. Reporting on Westfield’s upcoming float, on April 14, 1960, The Australian Financial Review noted its Blacktown shopping centre, inwestern Sydney,was “one of the first of its kind in Australia”.

Lowy and Saunders were innovators and early adopters.

“Often John would arrive in the morning with a scrap of paper torn out of the Financial Review. We were hungry for new ideas,” says Lowy. Their partnership lasted about 30 years and for the next 30, Lowy was at the helm of Westfield, which at one point – on some metrics – became the largest retail property group in the world.

When he sold it to the French mall giant Unibail-Rodamco for $32 billion, he achieved the unusual feat of co-founding and selling an ASX top 20 company in one generation. While widely complimented on his sense of timing, privately he thought he’d probablywaited a bit too long.

In the years leading up to this sale, his life circumstances had changed significantly. His siblings and many close friends had passed away, two of his sons were living outside Australia and so were most of his grandchildren and all his great-grandchildren.

For almost two decades he’d been visiting Israel, reconnecting with people he knew from his past and growing a new social circle. When he and his wife, Shirley, built a house there, it turned them into semi-locals andwhen he rebuilt an existing think tank, focused on Israeli security, it plugged him into the higher echelons of defence, policy and politics. The centre of his life had gradually shifted and with the business sold in late 2017, he wanted to make the best of the time left. In 2018, he and Shirley moved to Israel.

People thought the salewas the family’s finale. Collectively, Lowy and his three sons had put more than 150 years into Westfield and had worked together like a businessmachine, relentlessly pushing forward. As they were no longer young, were geographically spread and without a central focus, it was thought they wouldn’t hold together.

“But we did,” says Lowy, “we said we would go private and transition from being operators to investors, and that’s what we have done. It required a total transformation of personal effort. It took us a while to get adjusted and although we’ve had our lumps, we work together very closely. We’re active but patient investors.We don’twant to sit on our laurels, and we don’t want lazy capital. This private business suits our capital, our cash requirements and our temperament.”

At one time, he was called Australia’s most successful postwar migrant and, for a long time, he has been one of its wealthiest men. In 2010, he topped the Financial Review Rich List and this year ranked ninth with an estimated wealth of $8.51 billion. When he heard that, he laughed. “I’ll take half,” he said. It’s his standard response.

Run under the banner of the Lowy Family Group (LFG), the investment business has its headquarters in New York  and an administrative office in Sydney. As non-executive chairman, Lowy doesn’t actively invest but is in continuous dialogue with his sons.

In spite of COVID-19, with 60 per cent of their assets invested in global listed companies, 20 per cent in technology through private equity and 20 per cent in real estate, he says they have made considerable gains.

“This is a very serious investment management business, with a formal structure, weekly reports, regulations and other obligations. Some of my grandchildren are involved too, alone or in partnerships with their cousins. This way, the equity is well used.

“The work is not for show, not for publicity and not for recognition. It’s direct reward for effort. It’s so much easier not being responsible for other people’s money. The secret is continuity. Ironing out lumps is a continual process. You never eliminate them completely but you reach a reasonable compromise. There’s no room for stubbornness. I have seniority but I use it extremely rarely and with great care.”

The family loves football analogies and, in business, one of its rules is to play the ball, never the man. Where once Lowy was captain, they say he’s now coach.

It was soccer, not business, that for a time made him an Australian folk hero. The sport was close to collapse in 2003 when then prime minister John Howard asked him to rebuild it. “And I did,with both hands,” he says. “The country embraced it, followed it, supported it and attended the games – and it boomed, going from insolvency to revenue of around $100 million a year.”

In 2006, when he got the Socceroos to the FIFAWorld Cup for the first time in 32 years, the country exploded. After that, when he attended local games, supporters would surround his car chanting “Frankie, Frankie!” At the height of their enthusiasm, they tookupthe call “Frankie forprimeminister”.

Israel has a culture of respect for elders and particularly for the dwindling number of veterans from its 1948War of Independence. Lowy is such a veteran and says while he’s usually the oldest in the room, it’s not material.

“Iwas born an oldman. In the drama ofwartime Europe, I remember no play, no real youth – just pain and persecution.

For me there was little opportunity, little schooling and, from 13, little family structure.”

At 15, he left Europe as an illegal immigrant, alone on a crowded boat sailing for Palestine. Just after his 17th birthday, he was in military uniform and a few months later was a member of an elite commando unit.

At 21, he decided to join the surviving members of his family who had migrated to Sydney and arrived urgently in need of a job to pay back the money borrowed for his airfare.

It was 1952 and later that year he met Shirley. In a private memoir, she recalled him having “a mischievous look coupled with a seriousness” she had not seen before. “From the way he expressed himself, to his ability to persuade others, to his readiness to work at anything, he was unlike anyone I had ever encountered. Where others sawblack and white, he saw gradations.”

Lowy was struck by the tranquillity of Australia and how no one stood in his way. “In those days, Australia was fairly insulated with the economy largely dependent on butter, wheat and wool. The influx of European immigrants was changing this dynamic and as the country broadened its outlook, so did I.” At 25, when he and Saunders began their building company, they were on the heels of other Europeans, particularly Albert Scheinberg and Ervin Graf, who founded Stockland.

Such was the country’s acceptance of European entrepreneurship that Lowy was not yet 30 when Westfield floated. “No one questionedmy age,my accent,my imperfect English, my religion or my lack of education. The future seemed wide open.”

But the population was small, and he and Saunders used to walk up and down the Rose Bay waterfront, worrying whether there would ever be enough shoppers to fill all the new malls they intended to build. So they looked to other markets. Having come from abroad, they had no fear of venturing outside Australia and by the late ’70s, they’d expanded to the US.

Lowywas also developing a taste for capital restructuring and, in 1980, pulled off one of the biggest deals Australia had seen, splitting Westfield into a holding company and a property trust, increasing shareholder value eightfold in the process. He was also dreaming of Britain, particularly of high-density London where people shopped on wet and windy high streets. Could he coax them into temperaturecontrolled malls where an upbeat atmosphere encouraged shopping? By 2000 Westfield was operating across Britain.

By 2008, it was in the heart of London, with the newest and biggest shopping centre in Europe. By 2010, its flags were flying on another mega-mall at the entrance to London’s Olympic site.

Westfield was always evolving and adapting. Along the way, it changed its goal from accumulating as many shopping centres as possible, to shedding the outdated ones and creating iconic malls. Capital restructuring happened again in 2004, when Lowy merged threeWestfield entities into one, creating a leviathan that survived the global financial crisis and emerged strong with a healthy war chest.

But in 2010 he split it and then, in 2013, announced he would progress that split, creating two distinct businesses. All the Australian and New Zealand assets would go into a new company called Scentre Group, while all international assets would go intoWestfield. This causedmayhem. People couldn’t understand it and, for the first time, the press rounded on him saying he was a bully, oppressor and intimidator. “I’d had plenty of criticism inmy career, it comes with the territory, but I’d never encountered such vengeance. I couldn’t understand why the mediawas playing the man,” he says.

In spite of this, the demerger went ahead in 2014 and created more than $10 billion in shareholder value. Things settled and in 2016, hewas opening a newWestfield mall – in the rebuiltWorld Trade Centre in New York.

It might sound ridiculous, but it had taken many years before he felt financially secure. His first sense of it was in 1998, when he sold down 30 per cent of the family’s interest in Westfield, realising almost half a billion. “Finally, I had private wealth,” he says.

David managed this and other familywealth through LFG.

It wasn’t intended nor apparent at the time, but the firstborn had begun building the bridge thatwould eventually take his father and brothers into new territory as private investors. These days, Lowy has largely abandoned the corporate uniform of his business career. The bespoke suits, tailor-made shirts and Hermès ties have given way to T-shirts and sports shoes. He has five chairmanships, all of which are conducted via Zoom, except for the two in Israel.  As honorary chair of the Israel Philharmonic Orchestra Foundation, it’s his pleasure to drive across town and sit around the table, without the obligation to fundraise. “I’d rather give money away,” he says. The Lowy Concert Hall is the orchestra’s home.

More often he’s at the leading security think tank in the Middle East, the Institute for National Security Studies, where he chairs its high-levelmeetings in Hebrew. This is his fourth language and to improve his expression and attune his ear to nuance, he continues to take private lessons.

While the INSS is politically agnostic, Lowy describes himself as a liberal democrat with an abiding interest in Middle Eastern politics and foreign policy. “This helps to keep me intellectually alive, active and socially engaged,” he says. He established the INSS in 2006 using experience he’d gained in 2003 while establishing a Sydney think tank, the Lowy Institute. It aims to deepen international policy debate within Australia and give this country a greater voice abroad. He gifted it to the nation to mark his 50 years in the country and continues to chair its board.

Unexpectedly, part of hisworkingweek is also spent on the periphery of science, through the Lowy Medical Research Institute. In Israel, it invests in two biotech start-ups, one of which is developing a “liquid biopsy” that uses body fluids to detect cancer. He’s very interested in this because it’s 10 years since he underwent a radical operation for bile duct cancer which, untreated, would have led to pancreatic cancer. Gratitude for the miracle of early detection and a gifted surgeon has never left him.

Having sat through 18 years of scientific meetings at the LMRI, he’s picked up bits and pieces and is increasingly intrigued by it. The institute was created after one of his sonswas diagnosedwith a little-understood eye disease. The family launched a global research program which has since made sight-saving breakthroughs for people with the retinal condition known as macular telangiectasia.

In the past three years, Lowy has been back to Australia only once, in 2019. COVID-19 completely ruled out last year, and he was hoping for this year but was deterred by quarantine. “I no longer have that many two-week periods left and I don’twant to be locked up for one of them,” he says.

He’s now on his boat in the south of France. Although he’s with friends and family, there is a hole in heart. Shirley, who had been growing increasing frail and losing her memory, had been nursed at home with all the comforts her husband could provide. In December last year, she passed away.

Before they moved into their house, Shirley had found and carefully replanted a 300-year-old olive tree to shade the front door. It was a project he never understood. Now, whenever he passes it, she’s with him.

“Life has dramatically changed for me, for the worse,” he says. “I am now a widower and a very sad one at that. After 67 years of being with her, nowbeingwithout her is the most difficult task ofmy life. I don’t quite know how to handle it. I don’t quite know how to be.” •

HEADLINE: A word from the editors
TEXT:
Paul Bailey: To start, perhaps if I could ask Colleen first,when you joined in the mid-1970s what were your impressions of the publication, the office and the people who were running it at the time?

Colleen Ryan: I had been in chartered accountingwhich back then was incredibly sexist towards women. So I left that and joined the Financial Review and took a 40 per cent pay cut, and was just delighted to arrive in an office where there was Max Walsh as editor, Fred Brenchley as deputy editor and Vic Carroll. There was amazing talent.

Of course, we had typewriters, smoking in the office, drinks at five o’clock and then drinks at eight o’clock, it was just a raucous place. No one got to work before 11 and no one left before nine. And it was also a time when theModest Member Bert Kelly was writing, and his was a big line that ran right through the Fin Review; no tariffs, free trade. The paper had a real voice in government policy. But I was very much a junior; I managed to get a defamation case in the first nine months with John Laws and wound up in the witness box. It was a fun time.

Bailey: And Alan, what were your first impressions?

Alan Kohler: IwashiredbyBobGottliebsen toworkwithhim on the Chanticleer column in 1979. I did Chanticleer for a few years and then Max Suich brought me to Sydney in 1984 as deputy editor. That was a bit of a baptism by fire, going to the Sydney office. Paddy McGuinness was editor-in-chief, Tony Maidenwas editor. Paddywas a force of nature, hewas incredible.

Greg Hywood: I was hired in 1976 by Trevor Sykes, head of the Melbourne office, and my first day really set up my expectations of what journalism was all about. I got in at 10o’clockandTrevor said toBobMills,whowas the industrial relations writer, “Take Greg to the branch office.” I thought we were going to go around to a little office in Collins Street at the stock exchange. And instead, we went down the hill into the front bar of the Grosvenor Hotel.

So, we were there by three minutes past 10 and they kept me in the bar all day, in shifts. Trevor came down and had a couple of beers, and then Bob and then the various stars of the place in Melbourne. They kept me there until five in the afternoon and Trevor then sort of pushed me, I was absolutely goat-faced, obviously, he pushedme out and said, “Well today we’ve taught you to drink. Tomorrow we’ll teach you to type.”Which of course they never did.

And it was so indicative of the times: “revenue will look after itself, we’re about the journalism”. It was a drinking culture, and it was a fun culture but it was also a deadly   AlanKohler EDITOR 1985 1988 Paul Bailey EDITOR 2011 Present Michael Stutchbury EDITOR IN CHIEF 2011 Present serious culture givenwhatwewere doing. Youwere standing on the shoulders of giants, people like Max Newton and Vic Carroll and Max Walsh. They had set up this notion of editorial independence, which they had to fight for. Vic actually had to fight and got sacked over various disputes he had with the Fairfax family, and it really wasn’t until 1977 that that editorial independence came into its own after James Fairfax became chairman.

And so it was a unique place full of very strong-willed people and the Financial Review had this notion of what the world should be, which was a free, open, anti-protectionist economy. It’s like Colleen said, they pushed that very, very hard and really changed Australia over the course of many years. And I think that was the foundation and substance of the Fin Review.

Paul Bailey: And Alan,when you took over as deputy editor and then as editor, it was the mid-1980s. It was a time of major economic reform. What was it like to run the paper during that time?

Kohler: It was incredible. I arrived in Sydney in 1984, a year after the dollar was floated. Keating and Hawke were in full flight. After I was made editor in ’85, Imade an appointment to go and see Keating in Canberra. I showed up at his office and waited for him. He showed up at 12 and said, “Listen, let’s go and have some lunch.” We were at lunch until five o’clock and it set up this fantastic relationship with Keating which I still have today. To talk to him through that timewas extraordinary, really. Unlike any politician I’ve seen since, he had a vision of what Australia needed to be and he wasn’t really concerned with polling. He wasn’t concerned with popularity. What he was doing was changing Australia and he knew it.

When he warned that Australia was going to become a banana republic, he did it from his mother’s kitchen on the phone with John Laws. And someone told me about it and we splashed the paper with it, and that became a turning point for the country. The Fin Review at that time was in the thick of it with what Keating was doing. Because, as Greg said, the Financial Review also had a vision which predated Keating and I think was tremendously influential in creating the right environment for Keating to dowhat he did. And I think he recognised that throughout the ’80s.

Bailey: Stutch, what was your of impressions of those times?

In the office, as the others have mentioned, there was a lot of drinking. Peter Maher, the mining writer, after lunch would have his head down on the typewriter. People would ring up to Sydney saying, “Yeah, he’s just filing the copy now” and someone else would file the copy for him.

And just like the others, I’mvery conscious of our heritage from the ’80s. You had the opening up of the economy, business was suddenly unleashed, much more competition, animal spirits, entrepreneurs. It all came together in the ’80s, and the Fin really performs strongly at that intersection between policy and business. It’s a really fertile area for us.

Bailey: Colleen, during your time John Howard was PM.

Ryan: Yes, when I became editor it was 1998 and John Howard had already been in for two years. We were just coming through the Asian financial crisis. One thing that really struck me about the crisis was how good the Financial Review’s coverage of the region was, because I was in Washington for the start of it and Australian newspapers don’t havemuch cache inWashington really. But Greg Earl’s coverage was so extraordinary that all of a sudden people would speak to me because they realised that the Financial Review had really top coverage and our region was under focus.

Editors reflect ColleenRyan EDITOR 1998 2002 GregHywood EDITOR, EDITOR-IN-CHIEF 1993 1998

But yes, I came in and therewas an election straight away.

Kim Beazley was the opposition leader. It didn’t look like he had much chance and as it turned out he didn’t. But then there was another election while I was editor in 2001, Kim Beazley thought he was a shoo-in and then Tampa and September 11 happened, and Howard was back in again.

Bailey: What were you trying to do with the AFR when you took over?

Ryan: Well, in retrospect I may have had the wrong approach. I wanted to broaden the paper, I wanted it to be on every coffee table in Potts Point. We had the business people onside and what we needed to do was broaden it out, because economics had become such an Australian pastime. And I thought I could really boost the circulation.

I think it worked; Greg had already started the Saturday paper and Friday Review which had broadened it out, and I was trying to take it further than that.

And that’s when we came up with the Power issue of the magazine. That was a really great thing and, I think, one of the more positive outcomes of my attempt to broaden the circulation. But then business wanted a much more business-focused paper, so I had to rein inmy ambitions.

Hywood: Well, the good thing about being editor of the Financial Reviewis the scriptwas sort of basically there. You continued the notion of what we’re about; free trade, we’re about no protection and thatwas determined. Whatwe had to do, however, was make the business work well. And the editor was in a very, very powerful position to do that.

I rememberwhenwe started theweekend edition against a lot of internal opposition from The Sydney Morning Herald.

That was a really important development for the paper because it then took it from a five-day-a-week business paper to something a bit broader. And the audience for the Financial Review has always been more discursive than people thought. It wasn’t just the corporate data dump and public policy and business news. The research we did in terms of the weekend edition found that 35 per cent of the readership were blue-collar workers who would buy The Daily Telegraph or the Herald Sun as their first paper and the Fin Review as their second. There was a lot of internal debate around whether or not the weekend paper would work, but it did.

Bailey:AndStutch,whatwas it likewhen youbecameeditor?

Stutchbury: On the content side, when I came in, in 2011, I wanted to make the masthead probably more of a business thing, more pro-business.

It doesn’t mean by any means that we’re the mouthpiece of business, but we basically assumed that business is a good thing, it puts food on the table, it pays the taxes. It doesn’t mean we’re soft. If you’re a Rio Tinto or AMP over the past year, you wouldn’t feel like we’ve been easy on you.

But I did make a conscious decision to make it more of a pro-business paper.

The other thing, when I came in, it really was the beginning of the great digital disruption. In the old days there were high barriers to entry for mastheads. Now there are much lower barriers to entry and a lot more competition. So what is our fundamental competitive advantage? Tome, the thing that can’t be replicated is the deep engagement with the business community over decades, seven decades as it turns out. No one can really replicate that and it extends to this day.

So you’re really a business community masthead with politics and other issues, and you’ve captured a certain audience.

In the old days of print theywould say if you’re going into a businessmeeting, “well, have you read the Fin Review this morning?” If you haven’t, that was your disadvantage.

To make that apply in the digital world has entrenched us into our core audience.

Bailey: Colleen, what were some of the bigger stories that you remember from your time?

Ryan: September 11. One of the things that Greg had done was focus on photographs. Because if you’ve got a business publication, your photos aremeninsuitswhich occasionally was pretty boring. We had this amazing pictorial editor, Greg Newington, who did bizarre photographs, you know; slightly related to the stories, but he had an incredible eye for photography.

When September 11 happened, it happened at 11 o’clock at night in Australia.We did get it on the front page for the next day, but it was the following day when we had the time to decide what’s the pictorial image we should put on the front page. And Greg Newington was convinced that it was the waiter jumping out of the building (see Page Ones, p16).

And there was a lot of debate over it, everyone got involved and eventually Michael Gill [the publisher] and I said “no, we’ll go with Greg”. And that was the image that won all the Pulitzers and all the awards. Itwas run inmost newspapers, major newspapers, but not on the front page. And the next morningwe had 150 people say theywere going to stop their subscriptions because they took it as us putting it there as an image of the market falling. And it really offended them.

Stutchbury: Can I say, Colleen, the 9/11 picture was a gutsy thing and sometimes you’ve got to tell it like it is. You are the lens of truth and that was a really good thing to do, I thought. It was confronting, but the whole thing was confronting, and you can’t shy away from it. I thought it was gutsy and good.

Ryan:Well thanksMichael, you’re one of the few.

Bailey: How did the Financial Review handle the shift to digital? Colleen, you were there at the start of that change.

Ryan:Well, the Financial Reviewwas one of the first to put up a paywall, that was done by Michael Gill. I can remember it wasmuchdebated at the time,butnowmostpeople see that’s the only way you can go. One of the big confrontations with business was when we pulled out of [the clipping service] Factiva. Everything in the Financial Reviewwas onFactivaof a morning. So, everybody had the Financial Review without actually having to pay for the Financial Review.

Once we set up the paywall, Factiva became a huge issue.

And it tookmonths and months of Michael Gill going to see these CEOs for them to finally realise that Factivawas eating our lunch. But at times it was all very frustrating. Some higher management levels let us down a bit, they did. But it’s a different company now.

Stutchbury: It’s been such an incredible disruptive period, this last 15 years. The Fin Review was a pioneer, as Colleen says, in putting up a paywall with a very high price point. To me, that was in part to try and protect the quasi-monopoly rents in print but then Alan [Kohler] attacked them through Business Spectator. So when I came and Brett Clegg came in [as publisher] under Greg [as Fairfax CEO], we brought the price down. Itwas still quite expensive though;we managed at least to set a high price point. And then Rupert Murdoch brought in his paywalls and the world changed.

The Fin Review pioneered the use of paywalls, in our own crazy sort of way. And we’re sold online at a premium price point, like the FT or Wall Street Journal, which we’ve been able to maintain through the whole disruption of the past decade, through the pandemic and nowdigital is 60 per cent of revenue versus print. Subscriptions are getting on to close to 60 per cent of revenue compared to advertising. So you’re building a business model based on selling your content directly to consumers.

The business model has transformed and not every time did we have it totally right or wrong. The laws of physics change but we’ve ended up in a place where we’re now in a growth stage.

Hywood: It’s interesting, starting back at the beginning on my first day when we went to the pub, everyone assumed that revenue was going nowhere, and no one could see the internet coming. Inside Fairfax we had to follow the Financial Review rules. We had to become a very efficient organisation, and we had to change the organisation to fit the new reality.

And that’s what the Financial Review is, it’s a really common-sense perspective of the world. What’s real and what’s not real. What do we have to do to have a vibrant economy, and what did we have to do to have a vibrant organisation? We had to really change the thinking inside the business. We’ve got to remember that Fairfax was an oligopoly if not a monopoly for decades, and it built itself up with a legacy of cost and entitlements which had to be unpicked to operate in the new world. That was a transformation which was very, very difficult.

If you throw back to what we learnt from those initial Financial Review editors, they wanted the world to reflect, and our organisation to reflect, an efficient, vibrant economy and theywould’ve expected us to do this to the organisation.

Kohler: I must say it’s to Greg [Hywood] and Michael [Stutchbury]’s great credit what they did. I mean, it wasn’t actually ever guaranteed that the organisation and the newspaper would survive. They have done a fantastic job transforming it.

Bailey: To pick up on Greg’s point, is there some sort of through-line of editors for the Fin Review, and how would you describe them? If you’re looking for adjectives youmight say feisty, opinionated, of course you’ve got to be opinionated if you’re an editor. It seems to me that the editors of the Fin Review have collectively held a sort of imagination about what Australia could be, should be and must be.

Ryan: Feisty is a good description for the editors of the Financial Review. If you go right back to Max Newton in the ’50s or ’60s, he was a real wildcard and a bit of a crazy guy, but really smart. Then through Max Walsh who was really feisty, Paddy McGuinness equally. I think we sort of toned down as we went through the different editors. It’s not easy in a way to be the business paper in Australia because it is quite a small market. You’re in the limelight domestically but not globally. You’re quite influential in policy so it’s a difficult road for editors to keep that independence, to push for openness and keep the readers involved at the same time so that you are financially viable.

Bailey: Alan, do you have thoughts on that?

Kohler: The legacy of the Financial Review, the early editors who precededme, McGuinness,Walsh, Newton, they’re still with the paper in some ways. The culture that was set up by those guys in the early days is preserved, it’s still kind of there, it’s incredibly strong. And possibly more so than other papers. The Financial Review has this kind of intellectual strength owing to its history that makes it kind of quite a big fish in a small pond. The Financial Review really has always punched above itsweight because of that intellectual history it’s had.

Hywood: I have absolutely no doubt that the Financial Review changed Australia. It was the mechanism for this anti- protection debate to be delivered. And the people like Bert Kelly, the Modest Member, Max Walsh, every subsequent editor has followed this really sustained vision. And in the ’80s it wasn’t just Keating, it was Howard as well; there was a level of bipartisanship because the debate had been won.

The Financial Review had carried the debate and the debate had been won and was finally delivered.

And then things got wobbly, things got complicated in the world and that commitment in politics to reform has not been sustained. But the Financial Review has continued that vision, has continued to keep the pressure up. I think it’s been a vehicle for the transformation of the country. And everybody has participated. As an editor youwould go into a news conference, and you would have a perspective of what you think you wanted to deliver that day or that week. But it would change through the course of the conversation, for the better. And I think that the culture of the sharing of ideas is also something that those initial editors delivered.

Stutchbury: As editor-in-chief I’m very conscious of this heritage that we’ve been talking about. And the role of editor has changed to a certain degree. Traditionally, in the old days, editorswere more or less benevolent dictatorswho could rule the whole thing. Now it’s harder to control. The audience in a way has more power, if you like. The audience dictates a lot of some things of what you’re doing in the digital world. But that said, I think it’s still very important, especially for a masthead that needs to know what it’s on about, that needs to present a proposition to its audience, the editor has to really provide an intellectual framework about what it is we’re on about. What do we think is important? How do we determine what are the big things that are happening?

And the audience wants that. You just can’t say “well, everybodyisclickingonthathousepricestorysolet’sdomore of that”. People want you to provide your curated expertise about how the world operates and the important things for their careers, their investments, their businesses and also for the nation, for the general prosperity of the nation. The editor really does have to provide that framework and to be constantly in the newsroom to maintain the sharpness of the news-gathering and the news-breaking.

Bailey: I think we’re just on time there. Does anyone else want to jump in andmake any other points?

Stutchbury: I’ll say for the record the journos work a hell of a lot harder these days. They don’t rock up at 11am and go to lunch.

Hywood: That is complete nonsense

HEADLINE: Other Passions
TEXT:
“Once you’re done, you’re done. It’s a bit like a fashion show – get me out of here.”

So, Genevieve, you’re a puzzler?

Is that the name? Is that what we’re called?

Actually, it’s “dissectologist” if we’re being technical. But: your hobby is jigsaw puzzles?

Yes. My family and I started in lockdown last year, at the urging of my son [aged 9].

It’s a family activity but also, not. We leave them on the coffee table in the living room and everyone dips in and out, adding pieces here and there. It’s been a very nice distraction from … you know, everything.

What’s the biggest puzzle you’ve attempted?

We’re bound, literally, by the coffee table.

So I’d say 1000 pieces.

Are you good at them?

I don’t know. But I do like problem solving, and this definitely fits the bill. Puzzles are a good reminder of the value of stepping away and seeing the bigger picture to answer a question. Often after a day at work trying to figure something out, I’ll be driving home and realise, ‘oh, that’s how I do that.’ You take a step back, you get some perspective.

You’re currently in lockdown. I’m guessing a daily commute is off the cards.

Yes. I mean sometimes I will get up in the morning and start working straight away.

Suddenly it’s 5pm and the whole day has gotten away from you. I have been using puzzles as a break, to refresh my brain.

Are you competitive, as a family, or is it a team effort?

A team effort. It’s funny, the pieces other people see that you can’t. Sometimes I’ll be reading a book and I’ll look across to see that my 13-year-old daughter has finished a whole section. That’s quite cool.

You must have quite a collection of puzzles?

Oh, no! Once you’re done, you’re done. It’s a bit like a fashion show – get me out of here. We pass them on to friends. Some of them are quite beautiful though, so it feels a shame to pack them up. Right now we’re working on a puzzle of Frida Kahlo – it’s absolutely divine.

What’s the trickiest puzzle you’ve tackled?

We did a gradient puzzle and that was challenging. It was a picture of sunset, lots of lovely gingery pinks, oranges, yellows. It was difficult but I am obsessed with colour so I found it quite relaxing. We’ve also done one based on a Yayoi Kusama print, which was – pardon the pun – puzzling.

All those polka dots ... that took a while.

Do you have a starting strategy? Corners first?

I generally group into colour first – like if it’s the sea, you find the blue. I put them in piles and then start on a section.

It must be nice to have something to do together, as a family?

Absolutely. I never would have picked it up on my own, but it’s nice, when you spend all day at a screen or in meetings, to do something with your hands. And there is a real satisfaction in seeing it finished at the end. Except, of course, when there’s a piece missing. That really does drive me crazy.

That feels like a metaphor for our times.

Oh, yeah. You can’t pass them on when there’s a piece missing, it’s cruel. I think the dog eats them. And yes, there’s a whole other story there, too, with missing pieces.

The psychology of that is a different kind of rabbit hole, isn’t it? The existential crisis of the missing piece. •
